claims.text: In equiatomic NiCoFeCrMn and its controlled derivatives, local lattice distortion caused by atomic-size mismatch is the dominant factor governing yield strength.
Local lattice distortion is a dominant factor governing deformation behavior.
Lattice distortion strengthens the alloys by impeding dislocation motion.
Alloys with enhanced lattice distortion will have higher yield strength than the baseline equiatomic alloy.
Enhanced lattice distortion will alter strain hardening and ductility relative to the baseline.
Identical thermal processing will provide comparable microstructures across the baseline and modified alloys.
Partial replacement of Mn with Cu or Ti can introduce systematically different degrees of atomic-size mismatch.
Local lattice distortion will manifest as XRD diffraction-peak broadening.
Nanoscale chemical inhomogeneities are a manifestation or indicator of the proposed local lattice distortions.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch increases local lattice strain fields.
Local lattice strain fields act as barriers to dislocation glide.
The barriers to dislocation glide raise yield strength.
Localized stress concentrations and dislocation pile-ups modify strain hardening or ductility.
Increasing atomic-size mismatch will produce a measurable increase in lattice distortion.
Measured lattice distortion will correlate systematically with higher yield strength after correction for short-range ordering effects.
The unmodified equiatomic NiCoFeCrMn baseline has minimal atomic-size mismatch.
The baseline is expected to have lower lattice distortion, lower yield strength, and more homogeneous deformation than the modified variants.
The proposed relationship should hold when mixing entropy, temperature, strain rate, and other microstructural factors are controlled.
